No, histologic chorioamnionitis does not always correspond to clinical chorioamnionitis. Histologic chorioamnionitis refers to the presence of inflammatory cells in the placental tissues, which can be detected through microscopic examination. Clinical chorioamnionitis, on the other hand, refers to the presence of symptoms such as fever, uterine tenderness, and fetal tachycardia, which indicate an intrauterine infection.

Studies have shown that not all cases of histologic chorioamnionitis are associated with clinical symptoms, and conversely, not all cases of clinical chorioamnionitis have evidence of histologic chorioamnionitis. This discrepancy can be due to various factors, such as the timing and severity of the infection, the presence of other underlying conditions, and the sensitivity of the diagnostic tests used.

Therefore, while there is some correlation between histologic and clinical chorioamnionitis, they are not identical entities, and a diagnosis of one does not necessarily imply the presence of the other.
